authors: Chun, Jon and Schroeder de Witt, Christian and Elkins, Katherine
title: Comparative Global AI Regulation: Policy Perspectives from the EU, China, and the US
what_it_says: Compares AI regulation in the EU, China and the US, with attention to US federal and state approaches including California SB 1047. Argues the regimes reflect different cultural, political and economic outlooks on safety versus innovation and influence one another.
why_relevant: A recent comparative study of the jurisdictions whose provisions the evidence table codes.

authors: Al-Maamari, Amir
title: Between Innovation and Oversight: A Cross-Regional Study of AI Risk Management Frameworks in the EU, U.S., UK, and China
what_it_says: Compares how the EU, US, UK and China classify AI risk, enforce compliance, structure oversight and handle transparency. Finds the EU emphasises transparency and conformity assessment, the US and UK are flexible but risk fragmentation, and China is centralised with limited external oversight.
why_relevant: Directly comparable cross-jurisdiction study that touches conformity assessment, the closest topic to pre-deployment testing.

authors: Du, Jian
title: Toward Responsible and Beneficial AI: Comparing Regulatory and Guidance-Based Approaches
what_it_says: Uses qualitative content analysis of primary documents from 2017 to 2024 to compare AI governance frameworks of the EU, the US, China and IEEE. Identifies three governance models and proposes a hybrid framework.
why_relevant: Precedent for coding governance documents by content analysis and for separating binding rules from guidance.

authors: Roberts, Huw and Ziosi, Marta and Osborne, Cailean and Saouma, Lama
title: A Comparative Framework for AI Regulatory Policy
venue_or_publisher: International Centre of Expertise on Artificial Intelligence in Montreal (CEIMIA)
what_it_says: Proposes a seven category framework for analysing how governments regulate AI and applies it to Canada, China, the EU, the UK and the USA. Finds the EU and Canada favour centralised horizontal hard law while the others use more sector specific, lighter touch measures.
why_relevant: A coding framework for comparing regulatory approaches, relevant to the paper's own coding scheme.

title: National AI policies & strategies
what_it_says: Online database of national AI policy initiatives covering more than 1,000 initiatives from 69 countries, territories and the EU, browsable by country, policy instrument and target group. The page shows an access date of 17/11/2024; the year 2021 is taken from its citation line.
why_relevant: The main existing tracker of national AI policy, against which a provision level evidence table can be positioned.

title: The 2025 AI Index Report
venue_or_publisher: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (Stanford HAI)
what_it_says: Landing page for the annual report; its Chapter 6 teaser says advancing AI capabilities have drawn policymakers' attention and AI related policies are rising worldwide. Specific regulatory findings were not on the page.
why_relevant: Standard annual source for counts and trends in AI policy; a baseline for describing the policy landscape.

authors: Raji, Inioluwa Deborah and Smart, Andrew and White, Rebecca N. and Mitchell, Margaret and Gebru, Timnit and Hutchinson, Ben and Smith-Loud, Jamila and Theron, Daniel and Barnes, Parker
title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
what_it_says: Argues external audits happen after deployment and leave developers without ways to find harms earlier. Proposes an internal auditing framework spanning the development lifecycle whose stage documents combine into an audit report.
why_relevant: Foundational internal audit framework that frames pre-deployment testing as an accountability practice.

authors: Birhane, Abeba and Steed, Ryan and Ojewale, Victor and Vecchione, Briana and Raji, Inioluwa Deborah
title: AI auditing: The Broken Bus on the Road to AI Accountability
venue_or_publisher: IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML) 2024 (to appear, per arXiv listing)
what_it_says: Sorts AI audit work by the actors who do it and finds that only some audits achieve their accountability aims. Identifies the design, methods and institutional context that make audits effective.
why_relevant: Explains why audit requirements on paper may not produce accountability, which bears on reading testing provisions.

authors: Casper, Stephen and Ezell, Carson and Siegmann, Charlotte and Kolt, Noam and others (21 authors listed on page)
title: Black-Box Access is Insufficient for Rigorous AI Audits
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated on page)
what_it_says: Examines limits of audits that only query a system and see outputs, compared with audits given access to internals or development information. Argues that audit results need disclosure of the auditor's access and methods, and discusses safeguards for deeper access.
why_relevant: Access level is a design feature that a testing provision can specify or leave silent; useful for the coding scheme.

authors: Mökander, Jakob and Schuett, Jonas and Kirk, Hannah Rose and Floridi, Luciano
title: Auditing large language models: a three-layered approach
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated on page)
what_it_says: Proposes auditing at three levels: technology providers, pre-release models and LLM based applications. Argues this helps manage ethical and social risks while acknowledging the limits of auditing.
why_relevant: Places pre-release model testing inside a layered audit structure, a useful distinction for classifying provisions.

authors: Ojewale, Victor and Steed, Ryan and Vecchione, Briana and Birhane, Abeba and Raji, Inioluwa Deborah
title: Towards AI Accountability Infrastructure: Gaps and Opportunities in AI Audit Tooling
what_it_says: Maps the AI audit tool ecosystem through a landscape analysis of 390 tools and interviews with 35 practitioners. Finds most tools support evaluation and standards management while tools for harms discovery, audit communication and advocacy are scarce.
why_relevant: Evidence on the practical tooling that checklist or testing requirements assume exists.

authors: Shevlane, Toby and Farquhar, Sebastian and Garfinkel, Ben and Phuong, Mary and Whittlestone, Jess and others (21 authors listed on page)
title: Model evaluation for extreme risks
what_it_says: Argues for evaluating models for dangerous capabilities and for propensity to misuse them. Proposes building such evaluations into governance for training, deployment, transparency and security.
why_relevant: The main reference linking pre-deployment model evaluation to governance decisions.

authors: Liang, Percy and Bommasani, Rishi and Lee, Tony and others (50 authors listed on page)
title: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
what_it_says: Presents HELM, which maps use cases and evaluation criteria and evaluates 30 models across 42 scenarios on seven metrics. Releases prompts, completions and a toolkit and intends the benchmark to be updated continually.
why_relevant: Representative holistic evaluation standard that government testing guidance may reference.

authors: Reuel, Anka and Bucknall, Benjamin and Casper, Stephen and Fist, Timothy and Soder, Lisa and others (33 authors listed on page)
title: Open Problems in Technical AI Governance
what_it_says: Defines technical AI governance as technical analysis and tools that support oversight, gives a taxonomy of open problems and a partial catalogue for researchers and funders.
why_relevant: Situates evaluation and verification methods inside the governance problem the paper addresses.

authors: Anderljung, Markus and Barnhart, Joslyn and Korinek, Anton and Leung, Jade and O'Keefe, Cullen and others (24 authors listed on page)
title: Frontier AI Regulation: Managing Emerging Risks to Public Safety
what_it_says: Argues frontier models are hard to regulate because capabilities emerge unexpectedly and spread. Proposes standard setting, registration and reporting, and compliance mechanisms, with initial safety standards including pre-deployment risk assessment and post-deployment monitoring.
why_relevant: Names pre-deployment risk assessment as a regulatory standard, matching the provisions the evidence table codes.

authors: Feffer, Michael and Sinha, Anusha and Deng, Wesley H. and Lipton, Zachary C. and Heidari, Hoda
title: Red-Teaming for Generative AI: Silver Bullet or Security Theater?
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, 7(1), 421-437
what_it_says: Reviews industry red-teaming and related research and finds practices vary widely in goals, systems tested, settings and decisions informed. Warns that treating red-teaming as a cure-all risks symbolic security work and offers a question bank to guide efforts.
why_relevant: Supports treating mentions of red teaming in policy texts as underspecified unless scope and criteria are stated.

authors: Longpre, Shayne and Kapoor, Sayash and Klyman, Kevin and Ramaswami, Ashwin and Bommasani, Rishi and others (23 authors listed on page)
title: Position: A Safe Harbor for AI Evaluation and Red Teaming
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 235:32691-32710
what_it_says: Says researchers who test generative AI fear account suspension or legal action because company policies can penalise good faith testing. Urges developers to give legal and technical protections for public interest safety research.
why_relevant: Shows that who may test, and under what protection, is itself a governance question for testing provisions.

authors: Bengio, Yoshua and Mindermann, Sören and Privitera, Daniel and Besiroglu, Tamay and Bommasani, Rishi and others (about 100 authors listed on page)
title: International AI Safety Report
what_it_says: Synthesises current research on advanced AI capabilities, risks and ways to make systems safer, produced by about 100 independent experts at the request of countries attending the Bletchley summit.
why_relevant: Intergovernmental evidence base for what safety evaluation can and cannot currently establish.

authors: Perez, Ethan and Huang, Saffron and Song, Francis and Cai, Trevor and Ring, Roman and Aslanides, John and Glaese, Amelia and McAleese, Nat and Irving, Geoffrey
title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
what_it_says: Uses one language model to generate test cases that elicit harmful replies from another, scored by an offensive content classifier. Found tens of thousands of offensive responses from a 280B parameter chatbot and other harms such as leaked training data.
why_relevant: Technical basis for automated red teaming, which some provisions mention without defining.

authors: Weidinger, Laura and Rauh, Maribeth and Marchal, Nahema and Manzini, Arianna and Hendricks, Lisa Anne and others (13 authors listed on page)
title: Sociotechnical Safety Evaluation of Generative AI Systems
what_it_says: Proposes a three layer framework of capability, human interaction and systemic impact evaluation, surveys existing safety evaluations and identifies three gaps in current practice.
why_relevant: Gives a layered vocabulary for what a pre-deployment test is evaluating, usable as a coding dimension.

authors: Phuong, Mary and Aitchison, Matthew and Catt, Elliot and Cogan, Sarah and Kaskasoli, Alexandre and others (27 authors listed on page)
title: Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities
what_it_says: Introduces dangerous capability evaluations on persuasion and deception, cyber security, self-proliferation and self-reasoning and pilots them on Gemini 1.0 models. Finds no strong dangerous capabilities but some early warning signs.
why_relevant: Example of a developer run pre-deployment evaluation of the kind safety frameworks require.

authors: Veale, Michael and Zuiderveen Borgesius, Frederik
title: Demystifying the Draft EU Artificial Intelligence Act
what_it_says: Explains the April 2021 AI Act proposal using research on AI practices and EU product safety regulation. Finds the risk tiers sensible but argues some provisions have unexpected effects and that enforcement and maximum harmonisation raise concerns.
why_relevant: Early critical account of conformity assessment and standards under the AI Act.

authors: Mokander, Jakob and Axente, Maria and Casolari, Federico and Floridi, Luciano
title: Conformity Assessments and Post-market Monitoring: A Guide to the Role of Auditing in the Proposed European AI Regulation
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (journal not named on page)
what_it_says: Explains conformity assessment and post-market monitoring in the proposed AI Act in auditing terms. Argues the Act aims to create a continent wide auditing ecosystem and recommends seven amendments, including checkable criteria and safeguards for self-conducted checks.
why_relevant: Directly addresses conformity assessment and the weakness of self assessment.

authors: Gornet, Mélanie and Maxwell, Winston
title: The European approach to regulating AI through technical standards
what_it_says: Examines how the AI Act borrows harmonised standards and CE marking from product safety and extends them to fundamental rights. Argues standards cannot certify compliance with rights that depend on context and judicial determination, though they can encourage good governance practice.
why_relevant: Core critique of harmonised standards as a route to demonstrating testing compliance.

authors: Wachter, Sandra
title: Limitations and Loopholes in the EU AI Act and AI Liability Directives: What This Means for the European Union, the United States, and Beyond
what_it_says: Argues lobbying weakened the AI Act, which relies heavily on self-regulation, self-certification, weak oversight and broad exemptions. Also argues the liability directives cover mainly material harm and propose ways to close gaps.
why_relevant: Supports the paper's concern with self assessment and exemptions in testing obligations.

authors: Tabassi, Elham
title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
venue_or_publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST AI 100-1)
what_it_says: Landing page describes a voluntary framework to help organisations that design, develop, deploy or use AI identify and manage AI risks across sectors. The page did not itself describe the framework functions or testing, evaluation, verification and validation.
why_relevant: The primary US reference that testing provisions elsewhere are often benchmarked against.

authors: Gilardi, Fabrizio and Alizadeh, Meysam and Kubli, Maël
title: ChatGPT Outperforms Crowd-Workers for Text-Annotation Tasks
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (DOI shown on page: PNAS)
what_it_says: On 2,382 tweets, ChatGPT zero shot accuracy beat crowd workers on four of five annotation tasks and showed higher intercoder agreement than both crowd workers and trained annotators, at about one twentieth the cost.
why_relevant: Evidence used to justify LLM first pass coding of provisions.

authors: Ziems, Caleb and Held, William and Shaikh, Omar and Chen, Jiaao and Zhang, Zhehao and Yang, Diyi
title: Can Large Language Models Transform Computational Social Science?
what_it_says: Evaluates 13 language models on about two dozen computational social science benchmarks zero shot. Finds they fall short of the best fine-tuned classifiers but reach fair agreement with human labelers.
why_relevant: Calibrates expectations for LLM agreement with humans on text classification.

authors: Reiss, Michael V.
title: Testing the Reliability of ChatGPT for Text Annotation and Classification: A Cautionary Remark
what_it_says: Found ChatGPT labels of German website texts varied with temperature, instruction wording and repeated identical inputs, often below accepted reliability thresholds. Majority voting over repeated runs improved consistency; concludes validation against human labels is needed.
why_relevant: Motivates repeated runs and human validation when an LLM codes provisions.

authors: Törnberg, Petter
title: ChatGPT-4 Outperforms Experts and Crowd Workers in Annotating Political Twitter Messages with Zero-Shot Learning
what_it_says: Tests ChatGPT-4 on classifying the party of US politicians' tweets and finds it more accurate and reliable than expert coders and MTurk workers, with equal or lower bias.
why_relevant: Another data point on LLM versus expert coder accuracy in content analysis.

authors: Tan, Zhen and Li, Dawei and Wang, Song and Beigi, Alimohammad and Jiang, Bohan and others (10 authors listed on page)
title: Large Language Models for Data Annotation and Synthesis: A Survey
what_it_says: Surveys LLM based annotation, covering generating annotations, assessing their quality and using them for training, with a taxonomy of data types, learning strategies and open challenges.
why_relevant: Survey to cite for the state of LLM annotation methods and quality assessment.

authors: Savelka, Jaromir and Ashley, Kevin D. and Gray, Morgan A and Westermann, Hannes and Xu, Huihui
title: Can GPT-4 Support Analysis of Textual Data in Tasks Requiring Highly Specialized Domain Expertise?
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (DOI prefix indicates ACM; venue not stated on page)
what_it_says: GPT-4 given annotation guidelines performed comparably to well trained law student annotators on interpreting legal concepts in court opinions. Batch prediction cut cost with small accuracy loss; the model was sensitive to prompt formatting.
why_relevant: Closest evidence for LLM coding of legal text with guidelines.

authors: Guha, Neel and Nyarko, Julian and Ho, Daniel and Ré, Christopher and Chilton, Adam and others (40 authors listed on page)
title: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models
venue_or_publisher: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
what_it_says: Introduces a benchmark of 162 tasks across six categories of legal reasoning, built with legal professionals, and evaluates 20 open source and commercial LLMs.
why_relevant: Benchmark for how well LLMs handle legal text tasks like classifying provisions.

authors: McHugh, Mary L.
title: Interrater reliability: the kappa statistic
what_it_says: Explains Cohen's kappa as a correction to percent agreement for chance, ranging from -1 to +1. Argues Cohen's benchmarks are too lenient for health research and suggests stricter standards.
why_relevant: Accessible source for kappa interpretation thresholds and limitations.

authors: Artstein, Ron and Poesio, Massimo
title: Survey Article: Inter-Coder Agreement for Computational Linguistics
what_it_says: The landing page gave citation metadata only (no abstract was shown); the title identifies it as a survey of inter-coder agreement measures for computational linguistics.
why_relevant: Standard reference for agreement coefficients in annotation work in language technology.

title: Computing Krippendorff's Alpha-Reliability
venue_or_publisher: Departmental Papers (ASC), University of Pennsylvania repository (postprint)
what_it_says: Repository record (author field blank on the page) describing alpha as a reliability coefficient for agreement among coders, observers or instruments, originating in content analysis.
why_relevant: The usual citation for how Krippendorff's alpha is computed.

authors: Bujang, Mohamad Adam and Baharum, Nurakmal
title: Guidelines of the minimum sample size requirements for Kappa agreement test
what_it_says: Gives tables of minimum sample sizes for a kappa test at 80% power and alpha below 0.05. Finds required samples are much larger when marginal rating frequencies differ.
why_relevant: Directly addresses how many items are needed to estimate kappa, relevant to small coded samples.

authors: Hughes, John
title: Toward improved inference for Krippendorff's Alpha agreement coefficient
what_it_says: Proposes a better point estimator and a jackknife variance estimator for Krippendorff's alpha, giving interval estimates with much better coverage than customary bootstrap intervals.
why_relevant: Relevant to interval estimation for alpha when the number of coded provisions is limited.

authors: Wongpakaran, Nahathai and Wongpakaran, Tinakon and Wedding, Danny and Gwet, Kilem L.
title: A comparison of Cohen's Kappa and Gwet's AC1 when calculating inter-rater reliability coefficients: a study conducted with personality disorder samples
what_it_says: Compares kappa and Gwet's AC1 on 67 patients and nine raters in pairs. Finds AC1 more stable and less sensitive to prevalence and marginal imbalance.
why_relevant: Supports reporting an alternative coefficient alongside kappa when categories are skewed.

authors: Pérez, Jorge and Díaz, Jessica and Garcia-Martin, Javier and Tabuenca, Bernardo
title: Systematic Literature Reviews in Software Engineering - Enhancement of the Study Selection Process using Cohen's Kappa Statistic
what_it_says: Proposes iterating reviewer criteria until Cohen's kappa exceeds 0.8, after which reviewers screen separately. Reports about 28% time saving on 152 studies.
why_relevant: Shows kappa used as a calibration threshold in document screening with small numbers of items.

title: AI in the United Arab Emirates
venue_or_publisher: OECD.AI Policy Observatory (publisher inferred, not stated on page)
what_it_says: Country page that lists one national AI policy, the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence of 2031, announced in October 2017, aiming to make the UAE a leader in AI.
why_relevant: Tracker entry for the UAE strategy; a starting point for the UAE gap analysis, not an analytical study.

title: Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT
what_it_says: ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 wrote literature reviews on 42 topics and the 636 citations were checked against scholarly sources. Fabricated citations were 55% for GPT-3.5 and 18% for GPT-4, and both erred on real papers.
why_relevant: Quantifies fabricated references, motivating citation verification for this paper's own bibliography.

authors: Chelli, Mikaël and Descamps, Jules and Lavoué, Vincent and Trojani, Christophe and Azar, Michel and Deckert, Marcel and Raynier, Jean-Luc and Clowez, Gilles and Boileau, Pascal and Ruetsch-Chelli, Caroline
title: Hallucination Rates and Reference Accuracy of ChatGPT and Bard for Systematic Reviews: Comparative Analysis
venue_or_publisher: Journal of Medical Internet Research, 26(1), e53164
what_it_says: Tested GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Bard on reproducing references of 11 systematic reviews. Hallucination rates were 39.6%, 28.6% and 91.4% and precision was 9.4%, 13.4% and 0%.
why_relevant: Links hallucinated references to systematic review searching.

authors: Ji, Ziwei and Lee, Nayeon and Frieske, Rita and Yu, Tiezheng and Su, Dan and others (13 authors listed on page)
title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
what_it_says: Reviews how hallucination in text generation is measured and mitigated across tasks such as summarisation, dialogue and question answering, and in large language models.
why_relevant: General background reference for hallucination definitions.

authors: Agrawal, Ayush and Suzgun, Mirac and Mackey, Lester and Kalai, Adam
title: Do Language Models Know When They're Hallucinating References?
what_it_says: Treats fabricated references as an easy to check case of hallucination. Black-box consistency checks show models vary the invented authors across sessions for fake references but name real authors consistently.
why_relevant: Gives a cheap consistency check that could be used to screen suspect references.

authors: Liu, Nelson F. and Zhang, Tianyi and Liang, Percy
title: Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Search Engines
what_it_says: Human audit of four generative search engines found only about half of sentences fully supported by citations and about three quarters of citations supporting their sentences.
why_relevant: Evidence that citations attached to AI generated claims often fail to support them.

authors: Athaluri, Sai Anirudh and Manthena, Sandeep Varma and Kesapragada, V S R Krishna Manoj and Yarlagadda, Vineel and Dave, Tirth and Duddumpudi, Rama Tulasi Siri
title: Exploring the Boundaries of Reality: Investigating the Phenomenon of Artificial Intelligence Hallucination in Scientific Writing Through ChatGPT References
what_it_says: ChatGPT wrote proposals on 50 medical topics; of its 178 references, 69 lacked a working DOI and 28 could not be found by Google or DOI.
why_relevant: Early quantification of fabricated references in AI assisted research writing.

authors: Rao, Delip and Callison-Burch, Chris
title: BibTeX Citation Hallucinations in Scientific Publishing Agents: Evaluation and Mitigation
what_it_says: Builds a 931 paper benchmark and finds search enabled frontier models get about 84% of BibTeX fields right but only about half of entries fully correct. Grounding output in a deterministic retrieval tool improves accuracy.
why_relevant: Supports checking every field of a reference against a bibliographic source, not just existence.

authors: Naser, M.Z.
title: How LLMs Cite and Why It Matters: A Cross-Model Audit of Reference Fabrication in AI-Assisted Academic Writing and Methods to Detect Phantom Citations
what_it_says: Checked 69,557 citations from 10 commercial LLMs against CrossRef, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar and found fabrication rates of about 11% to 57% depending on model, field and prompt. Proposes cross-model agreement filters and a text classifier.
why_relevant: Large scale audit of reference fabrication and screening methods.

authors: Rao, Delip and Wong, Eric and Callison-Burch, Chris
title: Detecting and Correcting Reference Hallucinations in Commercial LLMs and Deep Research Agents
what_it_says: Finds about 3 to 13% of citation URLs from LLMs and deep research agents are likely fabricated, and releases an open source tool that separates fabricated from stale links.
why_relevant: Directly relevant to verifying URLs in AI assisted research claims.

authors: Remolina Leon, Nydia and Seah, Josephine
title: How to address the AI Governance discussion? What can we learn from Singapore's AI strategy?
venue_or_publisher: SMU Centre for AI & Data Governance Research Paper No. 2019/03 (working paper)
what_it_says: Examines Singapore's national AI strategy and Model AI Governance Framework, compares it with other jurisdictions and identifies challenges and gaps in AI governance discourse.
why_relevant: Scholarly account of the Singapore model used as a comparator.

authors: Lee Kok Thong, Josh
title: AI Verify: Singapore's AI Governance Testing Initiative Explained
what_it_says: Describes AI Verify as a voluntary testing framework and toolkit combining technical tests with process checks for self-assessment, run internally so data and models stay in the organisation's environment. Aims at verifiability, not defining ethical standards.
why_relevant: Concrete example of a government backed testing toolkit that is voluntary and self assessed.

authors: Harjani, Manoj
title: Where Is Singapore's AI Regulation Headed?
what_it_says: Notes Singapore has no AI specific law and relies on existing legislation and voluntary guidance, including the Model AI Governance Framework and AI Verify, which tests systems against 11 ethics principles. Questions whether this light approach suffices.
why_relevant: Recent commentary on a voluntary testing approach, useful when classifying such provisions as recommended not required.

authors: Spoor, Pat and Airey, Mark and Bennett, Cathy and Greensill, Julie and Williams, Rhys
title: Use of the capture-recapture technique to evaluate the completeness of systematic literature searches
what_it_says: Compared a Medline search with hand searching of one journal for trials from 1984 to 1994, using capture-recapture. Estimated about 160 publications in total with about 2 missed, recommends the approach for all systematic searches while warning that source dependence biases estimates.
why_relevant: Early demonstration of capture recapture for estimating search completeness.

authors: Airey CM and Spoor P and Bennett C and Williams R
title: Using the capture-recapture technique in systematic literature searches
what_it_says: Applied capture-recapture to a decade of one journal, comparing MEDLINE and hand searching: 115 trials found by both, 35 by MEDLINE alone and 8 by hand alone, with about 2.4 estimated missed by both.
why_relevant: Worked numbers for a two source capture recapture estimate.

authors: Motschall, E. and Rücker, G. and Antes, G. and Schumacher, M.
title: The number needed to read: are capture-recapture techniques feasible in searching literature for systematic reviews?
what_it_says: Tested capture-recapture models on a review searched across six databases. Estimates varied widely, and the authors conclude usefulness is doubtful because of manual duplicate identification and model selection problems.
why_relevant: Critical counterpoint on the reliability of capture recapture for searches.

authors: Stelfox HT and Foster G and Niven D and Kirkpatrick AW and Goldsmith CH
title: Capture-mark-recapture to estimate the number of missed articles for systematic reviews in surgery
what_it_says: Estimated about 3 of 40 included articles were missed in a trauma care quality indicator review, with database searches finding roughly 93% of known relevant articles.
why_relevant: Recent applied example of recall estimation for a review search.

authors: Kastner M and Straus SE and McKibbon KA and Goldsmith CH
title: The capture-mark-recapture technique can be used as a stopping rule when searching in systematic reviews
what_it_says: Tested a capture-mark-recapture model (Horizon Estimate) as a stopping rule for searching osteoporosis decision support literature across four databases. Concluded it indicates how close a search is to capturing the literature but needs more research.
why_relevant: Frames recall estimation as a stopping rule for searches.

authors: Kastner M and Straus S and Goldsmith CH
title: Estimating the Horizon of articles to decide when to stop searching in systematic reviews: an example using a systematic review of RCTs evaluating osteoporosis clinical decision support tools
what_it_says: Adapted capture-mark-recapture to estimate how many relevant articles lie beyond those found; the review captured about 68% of known articles with an estimated 592 missing.
why_relevant: Earlier source for the Horizon Estimate approach.

authors: Niwitpong, Sa-aat and Böhning, Dankmar and van der Heijden, Peter G.M. and Holling, Heinz
title: Capture-recapture estimation based upon the geometric distribution allowing for heterogeneity
what_it_says: Develops Chao's lower bound estimator for mixtures of geometric distributions and a censored likelihood estimator for population size from identification counts under heterogeneity.
why_relevant: Statistical background for lower bound population estimates when items differ in capture probability.

authors: Cormack, Gordon V. and Grossman, Maura R.
title: Engineering Quality and Reliability in Technology-Assisted Review
what_it_says: Shows quality defined by a recall threshold reduces to the probability of meeting it, and how any TAR method can be augmented to guarantee reliability at a known review cost. Tested on 555 TREC 2015 Total Recall topics, and proposes stopping criteria.
why_relevant: Recall estimation and stopping criteria in document review.

authors: Albous, Mohammad Rashed and Al-Jayyousi, Odeh Rashed and Stephens, Melodena
title: AI Governance in the GCC States: A Comparative Analysis of National AI Strategies
venue_or_publisher: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, vol. 82 (arXiv copy opened)
what_it_says: Document analysis of the six GCC national AI strategies (2018 to 2024). Finds the region relies on soft regulation through strategies and ethical principles, with no AI-specific law in any GCC state; AI rules sit mainly in data protection and cybersecurity law. Principles overlap with the EU AI Act but are less prescriptive; UAE and Saudi Arabia are the most aligned, and civil society has little role. Authors recommend stronger legal mechanisms and selective EU-style risk management.
why_relevant: Closest scholarly source on Gulf AI governance; supports the claim that UAE rules are non-binding principles, which motivates testing against stated provisions.

authors: Albous, Mohammad Rashed and Alboloushi, Bedour and Lacheret, Arnaud
title: The Future of AI in the GCC Post-NPM Landscape: A Comparative Analysis of Kuwait and the UAE
what_it_says: Compares public-sector AI adoption in the UAE and Kuwait using 62 policy documents, two UAE cases (Smart Dubai, MBZUAI) and 39 official interviews. Identifies four institutional mechanisms (centralised decisions, credible sanctions, pro-innovation narratives, flexible budgets) that move UAE pilots into services while Kuwait stays in pilots. Concludes efficiency gains serve social goals only with enforceable safeguards.
why_relevant: Peer reviewed evidence on how UAE institutions shape public-sector AI, relevant to where assurance of government AI would sit.

authors: Albous, Mohammad Rashed and Stephens, Melodena and Al-Jayyousi, Odeh Rashed
title: Artificial intelligence and the Gulf Cooperation Council workforce: adapting to the future of work
venue_or_publisher: Humanities & Social Sciences Communications (arXiv copy opened)
what_it_says: Studies whether GCC states are building the skills, incentives and governance matching their AI infrastructure investment, using six national strategies, 47 disclosed initiatives, and cases of MBZUAI and the SDAIA Academy. Scenario analysis suggests regulatory alignment may matter more than fiscal capacity.
why_relevant: Adds Gulf evidence that regulatory coherence, not funding, is the binding constraint; secondary to the governance paper.

authors: Al-Khalifa, Muneera
title: FALQs: AI Regulations in the Gulf Cooperation Council Member States, Part One
venue_or_publisher: Law Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis blog
what_it_says: Official legal-research overview for the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain. UAE: National AI Strategy 2031 with a governance goal, non-binding ethics guidelines (2022), a non-binding AI charter (2024), a 2018 interim-licence law, and an Abu Dhabi AI council (2024). Saudi: SDAIA ethics principles (2023) and generative AI guidelines (2024). Bahrain passed a standalone AI regulation law in 2024.
why_relevant: Authoritative, citable statement of what UAE instruments are binding versus non-binding.

authors: Singh, Shalabh Kumar and Sengupta, Shubhashis
title: Sovereign AI: Rethinking Autonomy in the Age of Global Interdependence
what_it_says: Models AI sovereignty as a balance of autonomy and interdependence across data, compute, models and norms. Applies it to India, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, describing state-led investment in Arabic-first models and sovereign cloud, and concluding that managed openness with guardrails is optimal for the Gulf cases.
why_relevant: Preprint context for why the UAE invests in Arabic-first models; not a governance analysis itself, so use sparingly.

authors: Sengupta, Neha and Sahu, Sunil Kumar and Jia, Bokang and Katipomu, Satheesh and others
title: Jais and Jais-chat: Arabic-Centric Foundation and Instruction-Tuned Open Generative Large Language Models
what_it_says: Introduces open 13B-parameter Arabic-centric models from UAE institutions. Describes safety alignment across five risk areas, guardrails in the chat interface, and urges adopters to run their own safety tests and keep human oversight for high-stakes uses. Links the work to UAE national digital and AI strategy and sovereign deployment.
why_relevant: Technical source for the Arabic-language side of UAE AI policy; documents developer-side safety claims, not policy.

authors: Metcalf, Jacob and Moss, Emanuel and Watkins, Elizabeth Anne and Singh, Ranjit and Elish, Madeleine Clare
title: Algorithmic Impact Assessments and Accountability: The Co-construction of Impacts
what_it_says: Traces the history of impact assessments and reviews AIA proposals. Warns that algorithmic impacts risk being defined as organisation-convenient metrics distant from real harms, and recommends treating impacts as constructed, anchored to actual harms, with affected communities and varied expertise involved.
why_relevant: Key scholarly critique of impact assessment as an assurance method for public bodies.

authors: Reisman, Dillon and Schultz, Jason and Crawford, Kate and Whittaker, Meredith
title: Algorithmic Impact Assessments Report: A Practical Framework for Public Agency Accountability
what_it_says: Proposes an assessment process for public agencies, loosely modelled on environmental impact review, to evaluate automated decision systems and judge acceptability. Notes agreed methods for fairness and safety in government algorithms did not yet exist.
why_relevant: Foundational think tank proposal for public-sector algorithmic impact assessment.

title: Trusted third-party AI assurance roadmap
venue_or_publisher: UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (GOV.UK)
what_it_says: Sets out UK government plans to strengthen the independent AI assurance market: a stakeholder consortium, a voluntary ethics code and skills framework, an assurance innovation fund, and a comparison of certification, process certification and accreditation routes, favouring professionalisation first. Published 3 September 2025.
why_relevant: Official statement of government AI assurance practice and who should assure.

authors: Zilka, Miri and Ashurst, Carolyn and Chambers, Luke and Goodman, Ellen P. and Ugwudike, Pamela and Oswald, Marion
title: Exploring police perspectives on algorithmic transparency: a qualitative analysis of police interviews in the UK
what_it_says: Interviews police staff and suppliers on the UK Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard. Finds transparency is achievable and could aid learning, but participants fear bureaucratic burden; recommends clear scope, exemptions, resourcing, supplier accountability, and future evaluation of whether reports meet user needs.
why_relevant: Empirical study of a public sector algorithmic transparency standard in use.

authors: Brand, Dirk and Hoffmann, McElory and Van der Merwe, Johan
title: Development of effective methods and tools for the auditing AI algorithms by Supreme Audit Institutions
venue_or_publisher: JeDEM - eJournal of eDemocracy and Open Government 17(3)
what_it_says: Proposes a framework for Supreme Audit Institutions to audit public-sector AI across its lifecycle, covering risk classification, data management and bias evaluation, grounded in openness, equitable outcomes, answerability and compliance. Argues generative AI needs dedicated guidance.
why_relevant: Recent peer reviewed audit framework for government AI, directly on public sector AI audit.

title: Understanding algorithms
what_it_says: Finds Dutch government algorithm use is growing while oversight lags; builds an audit framework covering governance, data and models, privacy, IT controls and ethics. Notes weak attention to ethics and citizen recourse, and recommends quality standards and continuous monitoring. Dated 26 January 2021.
why_relevant: Official supreme audit institution practice for auditing government algorithms.

title: An Audit of 9 Algorithms used by the Dutch Government
what_it_says: Applies the 2021 requirements to nine government algorithms; only three met all. Others showed weak performance and impact oversight, possible bias, data leak and access risks, and unclear responsibility for outsourced systems. Dated 18 May 2022.
why_relevant: Applied government audit of algorithms; shows what real public-sector testing finds.

title: Algorithmic Accountability for the Public Sector
venue_or_publisher: Ada Lovelace Institute, AI Now Institute and Open Government Partnership
what_it_says: Page describes a global study of first-wave policies for holding public-sector algorithms accountable, ranging from binding rules to principles and voluntary guidelines, drawing on practitioners' experience of implementing them. Page shows no date or named authors.
why_relevant: Think tank comparison of public-sector algorithmic accountability policies.

authors: Minkova, Kristina and Chakravarthy, Shashank M. and van Dijck, Gijs
title: Low-Resource Deontic Modality Classification in EU Legislation
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the Natural Legal Language Processing Workshop 2023 (ACL Anthology), pp. 149-158
what_it_says: Labels 200 sampled EU regulation provisions with six deontic classes (obligation, permission, power, prohibition, right, none) by three annotators. A small non pretrained fusion model beat fine tuned Legal-BERT on macro F1 (about 0.61 against 0.45), obligations dominate the data, and rare classes were not recognised.
why_relevant: Closest prior task to our binding status coding: clause level force labels on legislation with a small human annotated set and per annotator labels. We would cite it for the class imbalance point (report agreement and macro scores beside accuracy). It differs: it labels the modality of a sentence inside one legal family, while we code the force of a whole provision in guidance, standards and law, with a testing focus.

authors: O'Neill, James and Buitelaar, Paul and Robin, Cecile and O'Brien, Leona
title: Classifying sentential modality in legal language: a use case in financial regulations, acts and directives
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the 16th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Law (ICAIL 2017)
what_it_says: Classifies sentences of financial regulation as obligation, prohibition or permission using ensembles of neural networks over legal and general embeddings, and uses calibrated probabilities as a proxy for degree of obligation. Best accuracy reported is 82.33 percent on held out data.
why_relevant: Early example of modality classification in regulation that motivates why a modal verb rule is a natural baseline. We cite it in the baselines section. It differs: three classes, finance domain, no category for non binding recommendation or for ambiguous force. Only the abstract page was read.

authors: Brandsma, Gijs Jan and Blom-Hansen, Jens and Meijer, Christiaan and Moodley, Kody
title: Computational Identification of Regulatory Statements in EU Legislation
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (publication venue not stated in the text read)
what_it_says: Classifies sentences containing shall or must in about 120,000 EU legal acts as regulatory or not, using the ADICO institutional grammar, with 7,200 hand labelled sentences. A dependency parse rule approach reached about 0.80 accuracy and a Legal-BERT plus XGBoost model about 0.84, and the two disagreed often.
why_relevant: Supports a rule against learned model comparison on legal text and the caution that modal words alone do not settle whether a sentence regulates. We would cite it beside our wording rule baseline. It differs: it separates regulatory from non regulatory statements within binding EU law, while we grade force across binding and non binding documents.

authors: Sleimi, Amin and Sannier, Nicolas and Sabetzadeh, Mehrdad and Briand, Lionel and Ceci, Marcello and Dann, John
title: An Automated Framework for the Extraction of Semantic Legal Metadata from Legal Texts
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (extends a Requirements Engineering 2018 conference paper; journal not verified)
what_it_says: Rule based extraction over parse trees of modality (obligation, permission, prohibition), conditions and many other legal metadata types, tested on Luxembourgish traffic and other codes. Reported phrase level precision was about 97 percent and recall about 95 percent in one domain, and precision fell to about 82 percent in another. The final quarter of the text was not read.
why_relevant: Shows that marker lists for modality and conditions are an established method in requirements engineering, which supports our wording rule baseline and our conditional class (trigger words). It differs: French national statutes, modality limited to three values, no non binding category.

authors: Hassani, Shabnam and Sabetzadeh, Mehrdad and Amyot, Daniel
title: An Empirical Study on LLM-based Classification of Requirements-related Provisions in Food-safety Regulations
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated in the text read)
what_it_says: Classifies regulatory provisions by the requirements concepts they contain, comparing fine tuned BERT and GPT models, few shot GPT-4o, and simpler baselines (BiLSTM, keyword lookup). Fine tuned models beat the baselines, few shot raised recall but lowered precision, and generalisation to US provisions rests on only 50 sentences. The last part of the paper was not read.
why_relevant: Requirements engineering precedent for comparing language model classification of provisions with simple baselines and for reporting annotator agreement (kappa about 0.90 on one label). We would cite it for the baseline design. It differs: topic content labels in one domain, not binding force.

authors: Arnold, Zachary and Schiff, Daniel S. and Schiff, Kaylyn Jackson and Love, Brian and Melot, Jennifer and Singh, Neha and Jenkins, Lindsay and Lin, Ashley and Pilz, Konstantin and Enweareazu, Ogadinma and Girard, Tyler
title: Introducing the AI Governance and Regulatory Archive (AGORA): An Analytic Infrastructure for Navigating the Emerging AI Governance Landscape
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2024), vol. 7, pp. 39-48
what_it_says: Presents a curated and annotated dataset of AI laws and policies with a taxonomy of risks, harms, governance strategies, incentives and application domains (over 330 instruments at launch). The dataset documentation (also read) says documents are split into segments, tagged with a 77 code codebook and validated by a second annotator, with US federal coverage heaviest.
why_relevant: Most relevant existing segment level annotation of AI governance texts, so reviewers will ask how our table differs. We would cite it as the nearest dataset and as a source for locating documents. It differs: AGORA tags topics and strategies, not binding force or test type, and does not report row level verification against the source. Abstract page and dataset documentation were read, not the full paper.

authors: Guldimann, Philipp and Spiridonov, Alexander and Staab, Robin and Jovanovic, Nikola and Vero, Mark and Vechev, Velko and Gueorguieva, Anna-Maria and Balunovic, Mislav and Konstantinov, Nikola and Bielik, Pavol and Tsankov, Petar and Vechev, Martin
title: COMPL-AI Framework: A Technical Interpretation and LLM Benchmarking Suite for the EU Artificial Intelligence Act
what_it_says: Translates EU AI Act requirements into technical requirements tagged by system category and links each to existing benchmarks, then evaluates 12 language models. Some requirements (for example explainability, corrigibility) lack usable technical definitions, and the authors state the results are not legally binding.
why_relevant: Shows that mapping the Act to concrete tests is an active effort and that the Act leaves metrics open, which supports our reading that binding text seldom says how to test. We would cite it in related work and the discussion of what a provision requires. It differs: it operationalises the Act for one model type, while we record what documents say across families and how binding each statement is.

authors: METR (authors not named in the document)
title: Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies
venue_or_publisher: METR report (March 2025 update; first version August 2024)
what_it_says: Compares twelve company frontier safety policies and finds nine shared components, among them capability thresholds, evaluation timing and frequency, full capability elicitation and conditions for halting deployment. The policies are voluntary and the report counts presence of components without testing whether they are followed. The text read was cut off part way through.
why_relevant: Direct cross document comparison of what evaluation commitments exist, which we cite as the nearest comparison for the voluntary company layer. It is grey literature, so we would mark it as such. It differs: company commitments only, presence or absence coding, no force coding and no government documents. Reading was partial because the fetched text was truncated.

authors: Stelling, Lily and Murray, Malcolm and Galizzi, Bruno and Schaffelder, Max and Campos, Simeon and Papadatos, Henry
title: Evaluating AI Providers' Frontier AI Safety Frameworks
what_it_says: Scores twelve company frontier safety frameworks against 65 weighted criteria and finds scores from 8 to 34 percent. It notes that discretionary wording such as may consider is common for important actions and that frameworks work better as internal tools than external accountability. The last part of the text was not read.
why_relevant: Evidence that wording strength in safety documents is itself an object of study, supporting our focus on force. We cite it in related work. It differs: company voluntary frameworks, scored against a risk management ideal, not coded by force and test type across government documents.

authors: Marino, Bill and Hunter, Rosco and Schnabl, Christoph and Jamali, Zubair and Kalpakos, Marinos E. and Kashyap, Mudra and Hinton, Isaiah and Hanson, Alexa and Nazir, Maahum and Steffek, Felix and Wen, Hongkai and Lane, Nicholas
title: AIReg-Bench: Benchmarking Language Models That Assess AI Regulation Compliance
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint; also listed as a NeurIPS 2026 AI4GOOD workshop poster
what_it_says: Benchmark of 120 synthetic technical documentation excerpts, each rated by three legal experts for compliance with an AI Act article (Krippendorff alpha 0.651), on which ten language models are compared with the expert median. The best model reached quadratic kappa 0.863 and several models were more lenient than humans. Only the final few thousand characters were not read.
why_relevant: Most direct evidence on language models judging AI Act text with expert labels and moderate human agreement, which we cite in the coder agreement study discussion to justify reporting agreement between model coders and against the original coding. It differs: it judges system documentation against articles, we code the force of the regulatory text itself.

authors: Guliani, Keerat and Gill, Deepkamal and Landsman, David and Eshraghi, Nima and Kumar, Krishna and Gondara, Lovedeep
title: De Jure: Iterative LLM Self-Refinement for Structured Extraction of Regulatory Rules
what_it_says: Pipeline that turns sections of regulations (SEC, EU AI Act, HIPAA) into structured rules with a language model and language model judges that trigger regeneration. Quality is judged by models without reported agreement with human experts, and conditions and exceptions are the weakest part.
why_relevant: Representative of automatic extraction of rules from the AI Act, which we cite to say model extraction is possible but its checking is model based. It differs: no human check, no force classes; our design pairs model coding with blind second codings and a source check.

authors: Ariai, Farid and Mackenzie, Joel and Demartini, Gianluca
title: Natural Language Processing for the Legal Domain: A Survey of Tasks, Datasets, Models and Challenges
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated in the text read)
what_it_says: PRISMA based survey of 131 studies on legal NLP tasks, datasets and models, listing classification tasks such as deontic modality tagging in contracts and unfair clause detection. It notes datasets concentrate in EU, US, Chinese and Swiss jurisdictions. The last part of the text was not read.
why_relevant: Gives reviewers a general survey to anchor the claim that legal text classification is established while AI governance text is not covered. We would cite it once in related work. It differs: broad survey with no AI governance corpus.

authors: Bradner, Scott
title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels (RFC 2119, BCP 14)
what_it_says: Defines MUST as an absolute requirement, SHOULD as allowing valid reasons to ignore in particular circumstances, and MAY as truly optional, for use in IETF standards track documents.
why_relevant: Source for a formal definition of requirement levels behind a modal verb wording rule, and an example that conventions for shall, should and may differ between document families (this convention is not stated to apply to law). Not a scholarly article; page read in full, it is short.

authors: Reuel, Anka and Hardy, Amelia and Smith, Chandler and Lamparth, Max and Hardy, Malcolm and Kochenderfer, Mykel J.
title: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (also NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks track, per proceedings listing in search results)
what_it_says: Scores 24 AI benchmarks against 46 criteria across design, implementation, documentation and maintenance. Finds wide quality variation, with 17 of 24 lacking easy replication scripts and 14 of 24 not reporting repeated runs or statistical significance.
why_relevant: Cite in Related work as evidence that the evaluations whose use the documents mandate or recommend are themselves of uneven quality, so a clause saying 'test' does not fix test quality. Differs: it assesses benchmarks, whereas this paper codes what documents require, and it does not code metric or threshold content.

authors: Bean, Andrew M. and Mahdi, Adam and others
title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
what_it_says: Systematic review of 445 LLM benchmarks from major venues. Finds that about 48 percent of the stated definitions of the target phenomenon are contested and only 16 percent use uncertainty estimates or statistical tests; proposes eight practices.
why_relevant: Use to support the Interpretation paragraph that binding text seldom says how to test: even where a test is run, construct validity is often weak. Also a close methodological neighbour, since it used a language model for screening followed by manual review and reports moderate reviewer agreement (mean Brennan-Prediger kappa 0.524), which can be set beside our coder agreement. Differs: it reviews research benchmarks, not regulatory clauses.

authors: Weidinger, Laura and Raji, Deb and Wallach, Hanna and Mitchell, Margaret and Wang, Angelina and Salaudeen, Olawale and Bommasani, Rishi and Kapoor, Sayash and Ganguli, Deep and Koyejo, Sanmi and Isaac, William
title: Toward an Evaluation Science for Generative AI Systems
what_it_says: Perspective paper arguing that current generative AI evaluation is insufficient (static benchmarks with validity problems, audits that do not scale). Proposes borrowing from safety evaluation in transport, aerospace and pharmaceuticals, pairing pre deployment testing with post deployment monitoring.
why_relevant: Cite to frame why a table of where documents require testing matters: the science that would make a required test meaningful is still being built. Supports our coding of post deployment monitoring as a separate test type. Differs: it is a perspective piece with no document analysis.

authors: Rauh, Maribeth and Marchal, Nahema and Manzini, Arianna and Hendricks, Lisa Anne and Comanescu, Ramona and Akbulut, Canfer and Stepleton, Tom and Mateos-Garcia, Juan and Bergman, Stevie and Kay, Jackie and Griffin, Conor and Bariach, Ben and Gabriel, Iason and Rieser, Verena and Isaac, William and Weidinger, Laura
title: Gaps in the Safety Evaluation of Generative AI
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES), vol. 7, pp. 1200-1217
what_it_says: Reviews more than 200 safety evaluations of generative AI and identifies three gaps: few evaluations for non text modalities, uneven coverage of ethical and social risks, and a focus on the model rather than its context of use.
why_relevant: Peer reviewed precedent for coding evaluations by category and reporting coverage gaps, and supports our observation that some test types (content safety, human oversight validation) are thin. Differs: it codes research evaluations, not clauses in regulation or guidance, and has no binding force dimension.

authors: Raji, Inioluwa Deborah and Xu, Peggy and Honigsberg, Colleen and Ho, Daniel E.
title: Outsider Oversight: Designing a Third Party Audit Ecosystem for AI Governance
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the 2022 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES), p. 557
what_it_says: Compares third party audit systems in finance, environment and health regulation and argues that audits alone are unlikely to deliver accountability without deliberate institutional design.
why_relevant: Use in Related work for the third party audit ecosystem: our table records whether independent assurance is required or merely contingent (see the UAE paragraph). Differs: it argues from other regulated fields, while we count what AI documents currently say.

authors: Lewis, Dave and Lasek-Markey, Marta and Golpayegani, Delaram and Pandit, Harshvardhan J.
title: Mapping the Regulatory Learning Space for the EU AI Act
what_it_says: Describes the AI Act as a framework for learning and sketches a space of system types, protections and learning activities. Notes that compliance leans on CEN/CENELEC JTC 21 and ISO/IEC standards, that participation of SMEs, civil society and academia is limited, and that most Annex III systems rely on self certification.
why_relevant: Supports the claim in Related work that the Act leaves much to the provider and that harmonised standards carry the detail on how to test; also supports our limit that standards behind paywalls were read only as catalogue pages. Differs: it is a legal and policy analysis, with no clause level table. Year and venue are not shown in the fetched text; confirm before citing.

authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
title: Outline of Proposed Zero Draft for a Standard on AI Testing, Evaluation, Verification and Validation (TEVV)
venue_or_publisher: NIST AI Standards Zero Drafts project, outline for public comment
what_it_says: Outline of a high level TEVV standard loosely modelled on ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1, with clauses on terminology, concepts and governance and appendices of worked examples and a catalogue of methods. It is an outline for comment, intended to go to ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42.
why_relevant: Cite as a primary document that tells where the standards route for pre deployment testing is heading, and as a candidate row source for the table (check whether it is already a family member). Not scholarly and not peer reviewed; the date is inferred from the March 2025 project announcement and a September 2025 comment deadline.

authors: Gartlehner, Gerald and others (full author list not shown in the fetched text)
title: AI-Assisted Data Extraction with a Large Language Model: A Study Within Reviews
what_it_says: Prospective study within six systematic reviews (63 studies, 9,341 data elements) comparing human only extraction with model extraction plus human verification. Error rates against an adjudicated reference were 9.0 percent for AI assisted and 11.0 percent for human only extraction, with fabricated data at 0.8 and 0.5 percent.
why_relevant: Gives measured error and fabrication rates to set beside our verification audit error rate, and supports keeping a human in the loop. Differs: measures a verify-then-correct workflow on trial data, whereas our verifiers are also language models and our remedy (human second coding of 100 rows) is still pending. Preprint; check for a journal version.

authors: Pangakis, Nicholas and Wolken, Samuel and Fasching, Neil
title: Automated Annotation with Generative AI Requires Validation
what_it_says: Applies GPT-4 to 27 annotation tasks from 11 datasets and finds median accuracy 0.85 but median F1 0.71, with nine tasks below 0.5 on precision or recall. Sets out a workflow: codebook, human labelled random subset, comparison, codebook revision, held out check.
why_relevant: Strengthens the motivation for blind second codings and shows why we report percentage agreement beside kappa and F1 style checks. Our codebook then blind recode follows its steps; we differ in using language model second coders rather than expert human labels, which is our stated limit.

authors: Flemyng, Ella and Noel-Storr, Anna and others, on behalf of the joint AI Methods Group of Cochrane, Campbell Collaboration, JBI and Collaboration for Environmental Evidence
title: Position statement on artificial intelligence (AI) use in evidence synthesis across Cochrane, the Campbell Collaboration, JBI, and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence 2025
venue_or_publisher: JBI Evidence Synthesis 23(11):2162-2166 (published jointly in several journals)
what_it_says: States that AI in evidence synthesis needs human oversight, that authors stay responsible, and that any AI making or suggesting judgments (eligibility, extraction) must be reported with tool, version, purpose and limitations. Requires evidence the tool is sound, with piloting or calibration where needed.
why_relevant: Authority for our disclosure in the Ethics section and for reporting the model assisted steps in detail. We can state which items of its reporting list our paper meets and which not (for example tool version and dates). Differs: it is a position statement, not an empirical study.

authors: Gallifant, Jack and Afshar, Majid and Ameen, Saleem and others, Bitterman, Danielle S.
title: The TRIPOD-LLM Statement: A Targeted Guideline For Reporting Large Language Models Use
venue_or_publisher: medRxiv preprint; peer reviewed version in Nature Medicine (per note on the fetched page; details not checked)
what_it_says: A reporting guideline for biomedical studies using language models: a checklist of 19 main items and 50 subitems built by an expedited Delphi process, stressing transparency, human oversight and task specific performance.
why_relevant: Use as the closest best practice for reporting language model assisted methods; we can map our disclosure to its items in an appendix. Differs: aimed at studies that evaluate or deploy models in biomedicine, not at using models as research assistants for document coding. Cite the Nature Medicine version after checking it.

authors: Gebru, Timnit and Morgenstern, Jamie and Vecchione, Briana and Vaughan, Jennifer Wortman and Wallach, Hanna and Daume III, Hal and Crawford, Kate
title: Datasheets for Datasets
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint v8 (journal version believed to be Communications of the ACM 2021; not confirmed from the fetched text)
what_it_says: Proposes that each dataset ship with a datasheet answering questions on motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing, uses, distribution and maintenance. The authors say the process should not be automated.
why_relevant: Frame for the documentation of the evidence table itself: our repository records licence terms, retrieval dates and a decision log, and a datasheet appendix would map to those. Differs: it concerns machine learning datasets; our table is a research dataset about documents.

authors: Nosek, Brian A. and Ebersole, Charles R. and DeHaven, Alexander C. and Mellor, David T.
title: The Preregistration Revolution
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (venue and year taken from the DOI shown in search results, not from the fetched copy)
what_it_says: Argues that fixing questions and analysis plans before seeing outcomes keeps prediction and postdiction apart. Lists practical problems, including pre existing data, where blinding is often partial.
why_relevant: Supports our explicit statements that baselines and the keyword lexicon were written by an analyst who had seen the table, so they are not preregistered, and that the verification sample was drawn independently. Differs: we did not preregister the main analysis; the paper should say so.

authors: van Miltenburg, Emiel and van der Lee, Chris and Krahmer, Emiel
title: Preregistering NLP Research
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of NAACL 2021 (ACL Anthology 2021.naacl-main.51, per search results)
what_it_says: Offers preregistration templates for NLP work, including error analysis and resource papers with questions on sampling and annotator reliability, and notes that registration cannot prevent fraud or foresee every decision.
why_relevant: Peer reviewed precedent in the computational evaluation field for committing protocols before running them; we cite it when stating which parts of our protocol were committed with the code and which were not. Differs: it proposes templates and has no empirical test.

authors: Hofman, Jake M. and Chatzimparmpas, Angelos and Sharma, Amit and Watts, Duncan J. and Hullman, Jessica
title: Pre-registration for Predictive Modeling
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated in the fetched text)
what_it_says: Adapts preregistration to predictive modelling with a two phase template covering splits, metrics and baselines before training, and the model and test set statement before testing. In a study with six students it found people re-accessed test data after poor results.
why_relevant: Closest match to our baseline protocol (fixed folds, leave one family out, methods committed with code). We can cite it to explain the gap between a committed protocol and a true preregistration. Differs: it is for predictive modelling on fixed data, and we classify rows labelled by the same analyst.

authors: Li, Dan and Kanoulas, Evangelos
title: When to Stop Reviewing in Technology-Assisted Reviews: Sampling from an Adaptive Distribution to Estimate Residual Relevant Documents
venue_or_publisher: ACM Transactions on Information Systems 38(4), Article 41
what_it_says: Estimates the total number of relevant documents by sampling with replacement from an adaptive distribution with Horvitz-Thompson style estimators, and stops review at a target recall. Estimates tend to be low at low target recall.
why_relevant: Better developed alternative to capture recapture for our completeness check, which we describe as a simpler pilot against an independent reference list; it also shows why our estimate is likely to be an upper bound on completeness. Differs: it assumes a ranker over a known candidate pool, which we do not have for a sampling frame of policy documents.

authors: Alzubaidi, Ahmed and Alsuwaidi, Shaikha and Boussaha, Basma El Amel and AlQadi, Leen and Alkaabi, Omar and Alyafeai, Mohammed and Alobeidli, Hamza and Hacid, Hakim
title: Evaluating Arabic Large Language Models: A Survey of Benchmarks, Methods, and Gaps
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (Technology Innovation Institute, Abu Dhabi)
what_it_says: Reviews about 41 Arabic LLM benchmarks in four categories, among them safety and hallucination. Finds uneven dialect coverage, cultural misalignment in translated sets, no standard hallucination benchmark and roughly a quarter of benchmarks private or partial.
why_relevant: Supports our finding that no row requires language specific performance testing: the research side also shows thin Arabic evaluation. Differs: it surveys benchmarks, not regulatory requirements, and says nothing on binding force. Authors are at a UAE institute; note when citing.

authors: Peppin, Aidan and Kreutzer, Julia and Schoenauer Sebag, Alice and Marchisio, Kelly and others, Hooker, Sara
title: The Multilingual Divide and Its Impact on Global AI Safety
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (Cohere Labs); venue not stated
what_it_says: Argues that safety work and evaluation data concentrate on English and a few high resource languages, so safeguards are weaker elsewhere, and that translated safety prompts can lose their harmful intent. Recommends locally grounded evaluation data and transparency about language coverage.
why_relevant: Provides the rationale for coding language specific testing as its own question in the UAE section; Arabic appears only in passing as one of eight languages of a red teaming set. Differs: a policy primer, not a document analysis.

authors: Stelling, Lily and Yang, Mick and Gipiskis, Rokas and Staufer, Leon and Chin, Ze Shen and Campos, Simeon and Gil, Ariel and Chen, Michael
title: Mapping Industry Practices to the EU AI Act's GPAI Code of Practice Safety and Security Measures
what_it_says: Maps the safety and security commitments of the third draft of the Code of Practice for general purpose AI to quotes from company documents and finds that most measures have support from at least three companies, with gaps in areas such as external assessors and incident reporting. It does not assess compliance and uses a draft since revised.
why_relevant: Comparable quote based mapping from regulatory text to evidence, and a reminder that the Code is a voluntary route to the Act. We would cite it when discussing general purpose model testing. It differs: maps company practice to one draft code, not binding force across many regulators.

authors: Silva, Eryclis
title: Decoding Global AI Governance: A Computational Linguistic Analysis of National Regulations
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2024), student abstract
what_it_says: Analyses 1,065 AI strategy and legislation documents from 64 countries with text embeddings and a hedging measure, and reports that hard laws score higher on tentativeness than soft laws and that many documents resemble the EU texts. It is a short abstract with limited method detail.
why_relevant: A document level text analysis of hedging language across AI governance documents, so it is the nearest use of language cues for force. We would cite it and note it is a student abstract with an undefined measure. It differs: whole document similarity, not clause level coding.
